criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural and small-town piped drinking water service delivery systems (on-premises household/yard/institutional taps and off-premises kiosks and standpipes) in Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda, framed around pathways to universal safely managed drinking water access (SDG 6.1), though the empirical analysis evaluates operator revenue generation rather than user-level service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines institutional, governance, and administrative arrangements for rural piped water (public state-owned schemes with contracted private O&M and parastatal umbrella co-management vs private/social-enterprise build-operate schemes, tariff levels, and payment collection modalities). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines volumetric tariff rules ($/m3), cost-recovery/payment collection rules (prepaid electronic credit metering vs pay-as-you-fetch attendant collection and post-use monthly billing), and utility/operator ownership structures. (Note: while Criterion 2 is met under both readings, the study models operator financial revenue rather than a user access outcome, leading to exclusion under Criterion 4 under both plain and narrow Criterion 2 readings.)
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative longitudinal empirical analysis of more than 3,900 monthly operational records (2016–2019) from five piped water operators across Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda, analysed using ANOVA, t-tests, and generalized estimating equations (GEE).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4 (E04 Wrong outcome). All hypothesis tests and GEE regression models evaluate operator volumetric revenue ($/m3) and aggregate monthly service-area revenue ($/service area/month) as financial performance metrics. The authors explicitly report that user population counts are unavailable (preventing measurement of service area coverage/penetration or per-capita water consumption), that consecutive zero-revenue months were excluded even when water usage occurred because the study focuses on revenue generation rather than nonpayment/exclusion, that scheme reliability is unmeasured, and that actual end-user prices paid/affordability are unobservable. Descriptive monthly volume dispensed per waterpoint (m3/waterpoint/month) is reported in Tables 3 and 4 to normalize revenue and reflect waterpoint dispensing capacity, not as an evaluated user water-access or household consumption-quantity outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis (piped water service area-month, split by on- vs off-premises connection type), exposures (tariff level, prepaid credit vs PAYF/monthly billing, connection type, and enterprise vs public investment/ownership archetype), study outcome (operator volumetric revenue in $/m3), and study design (longitudinal panel GEE and archetype analysis) are clearly identifiable, while underlying user catchment headcounts are not reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: We extract, clean, and analyse more than 3,900 monthly records of volumetric water usage and revenue from user payments corresponding to the service areas of individual piped schemes operated by these agencies.

Payments are collected from users who access off premises connections by one of two approaches: the conventional PAYF approach, where users pay a standpipe or kiosk attendant when they collect water from the waterpoint, and the prepaid credit approach, where users pre-purchase electronic credit that can later be redeemed at the waterpoint.

Parameter estimates from generalised estimating equations (GEEs) are used to determine whether connection type and payment approach exhibit an association with revenue in each service area archetype while controlling for tariff level.
We acknowledge our results are aspirational due to this unavoidable bias because the study is focussed on understanding rates of revenue generation rather than rates of nonpayment.

Third, accurate data on number of water users over time are not consistently available. This prevents analysis of variables that are useful for deciphering revenue patterns such as service area penetration and per capita water usage across waterpoint connection types. We are therefore only able to examine aggregate water usage.

raw_response.exposure: Volumetric tariff level (2019 US$/m3 at PPP), user payment collection rule/modality (prepaid electronic credit vs pay-as-you-fetch attendant collection and post-use monthly billing), waterpoint connection type (on-premises vs off-premises), and infrastructure investment/ownership arrangement (enterprise build-operate vs public state-owned with contracted private O&M)
raw_response.outcome: Operator volumetric revenue from user payments (2019 US$/m3 at PPP, log-transformed in GEE models) and total monthly operator revenue per service area ($/service area/month), alongside descriptive aggregate waterpoint volume dispensed (m3/waterpoint/month)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Piped water service areas operated by 5 agencies (2 international NGOs operating as social enterprises and 3 private companies) in rural and small-town areas of Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda (2016–2019); >3,900 monthly records across 96 off-premises service areas (867 standpipes/kiosks) and 124 on-premises service areas (3,074 household, yard, and institutional taps)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although this longitudinal empirical study of rural piped water operators in Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda examines rule-type tariff levels, cost-recovery/payment collection modalities (prepaid credit meters vs pay-as-you-fetch and monthly billing), and public vs enterprise ownership/contracting models (satisfying Criterion 2 under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), its empirical outcome in all statistical tests and GEE models is operator financial revenue ($/m3 and $/service area/month). The authors explicitly state that missing user population counts prevent measuring service area penetration or per-capita water consumption, that consecutive zero-revenue months were dropped regardless of water usage because nonpayment is not studied, and that reliability and actual user prices paid (affordability) are unobserved. Confidence is set to medium because Tables 3 and 4 report descriptive summary statistics on aggregate volume dispensed per waterpoint (m3/waterpoint/month), though this reflects waterpoint dispensing capacity/throughput (mixing community kiosks, household taps, and institutional taps without user denominators) rather than an analysed user access or consumption-quantity outcome.
raw_response.study_design: Longitudinal observational panel and service area archetype analysis using generalized estimating equations (GEE), one-way ANOVA, and t-tests
